title: Seeing, Drawing and the Elements of Art

lessons.title: The Elements of Art
lessons.content:
All artwork, from a cave painting to a digital mural, is built from a small number of visual elements. Line is a mark with length and direction, and it can be straight, curved, thick, thin, broken, implied or expressive; it defines edges, creates pattern, leads the eye and carries feeling - a jagged line is restless, a horizontal line calm. Shape is a two-dimensional area enclosed by a line or an edge, geometric (circles, squares, triangles) or organic (free-form, as in leaves, clouds and human bodies), and positive shapes sit against negative shapes, the space around them. Form is three-dimensional: a sphere, a cylinder, a cube or the human figure seen in the round, or its appearance in a drawing where shading makes a flat shape look solid. Tone (value) is the lightness or darkness of a surface, from white through the greys to black, and it is the element that gives the illusion of form and light. Texture is the surface quality - rough, smooth, shiny, matt, grainy - and it may be real (tactile, as in a collage of sandpaper) or implied (a drawn suggestion of brick or water). Colour is the element of hue, value and intensity. Space is the emptiness around, between and within objects, and it is created in 2D work by overlapping, size change, placement, detail and linear or atmospheric perspective.

The elements do not work alone; they are organised by the principles of design - balance, emphasis, contrast, rhythm, movement, repetition, unity and proportion - which are covered in the next lesson. Learning to see analytically means naming what is in front of you in the language of the elements: which lines dominate, where the darkest tone sits, how the colour changes across a surface, what the light is doing. Most weak drawings and paintings are not the result of bad hands but of careless looking: artists learn to check every element deliberately rather than drawing what they assume is there. Squinting at the subject reduces it to masses of light and dark and reveals the structure under the detail; turning the drawing and the reference upside down, or viewing the work in a mirror, exposes faults the eye had accepted.
objectives: Identify and describe the elements of art in a given artwork
Explain how tone and space create the illusion of form and depth
Use the language of the elements to analyse your own and others' work

experiment.description: Element Spotter: Identify each element in a chosen artwork and label where it does its strongest work.

lessons.title: Drawing Skills and Observation
lessons.content:
Drawing is the foundation skill of all visual art, and it is learned by practice rather than granted by talent. The first habit is to draw from observation, working from the real object or person rather than from memory or a photograph, and to look more at the subject than at the paper. Proportion is measured by comparison: holding a pencil at arm's length to judge how many times a head fits into a body, or how the width of a jug compares with its height, and by using a viewfinder or a thumb and pencil to check vertical and horizontal alignments and the angles between points. Construction drawing builds the subject from simple forms - boxes, cylinders, spheres, cones - before detail is added, which keeps the structure believable; gesture drawing, done in a minute or less, captures movement, weight and attitude instead of outline, and contour drawing concentrates on the edge with a slow continuous line.

Perspective gives the illusion of three dimensions on a flat surface. In one-point perspective, parallel lines running away from the viewer converge on a single vanishing point on the horizon; two-point perspective uses two vanishing points and is used for buildings seen at a corner; three-point adds a third point above or below for looking up at, or down on, a tall object. Eye level is the key: everything at the viewer's eye level sits on the horizon line, objects above it are seen from below and objects below from above. Atmospheric perspective works differently, showing distance through fading contrast, cooler and lighter colour, softer edges and less detail - the effect visible in the blue hills of any Caribbean landscape.

Light and shade turn a shape into a form. A rounded object in directional light shows a highlight, a band of mid-tone, a core shadow where the form turns away from the light, reflected light bouncing back from the surface it sits on, a cast shadow, and often a small dark occlusion at the point of contact. Using the full range of tone, from the lightest white to the darkest black, in deliberate steps, gives form weight and presence; drawing only mid-tones leaves work flat and grey. Chiaroscuro - strong contrast between light and dark - creates drama, while high-key work stays in light tones. Good drawing practice also means working at different scales and speeds, keeping a sketchbook daily, copying from master drawings and from nature, learning to measure by eye, and accepting that error and correction are part of the process: the eraser and the re-drawn line are tools of observation, not marks of failure.
objectives: Draw from observation using measurement, proportion and construction
Apply one-, two- and three-point perspective and atmospheric perspective
Model form with a full range of tone and explain the parts of light on a form

experiment.description: Drawing Gym: Build a drawing from construction lines, check the perspective and add tone in five steps.

lessons.title: The Principles of Design
lessons.content:
Where the elements are the ingredients, the principles of design are the recipe: they describe how elements are arranged so that a work succeeds visually. Balance is the distribution of visual weight. Symmetrical (formal) balance mirrors one side against the other and reads as stable, orderly and sometimes static; asymmetrical (informal) balance uses different shapes, tones or colours on each side that nevertheless weigh the same - a large pale mass can be balanced by a small dark one; radial balance spreads weight around a centre, as in a wheel, a mandala or a decorated ceiling. Emphasis (focal point) is the part the artist wants seen first, achieved by contrast, isolation, position, size, colour intensity or detail. Contrast is the deliberate joining of opposites - dark and light, rough and smooth, large and small, warm and cool - and it creates energy and legibility.

Rhythm and movement refer to the way the eye is carried through a work. Rhythm is created by repetition with variation: repeated shapes, colours, lines or textures at regular or irregular intervals produce a regular, alternating, progressive or flowing rhythm. Movement is produced by directional lines and shapes, by the arrangement of figures looking or leaning, by repetition that draws the eye onward and by the gestures within the subject; in static media it is the felt sense that something continues. Repetition and pattern strengthen unity but risk monotony without variation. Unity, or harmony, is the sense that everything belongs together and the work is complete; it is achieved by limiting the palette, repeating shapes and colours, keeping surface treatment consistent and letting one idea dominate. Variety supplies the visual interest that prevents unity from becoming dullness - the two principles work as a pair.

Proportion and scale deal with relative size: the proportions of a figure, the relationship between the part and the whole, and the scale of the work itself, which changes how the viewer experiences it - a giant mural overwhelms, a miniature demands close attention. These principles are not rules to be obeyed but tools to be chosen. Artists sometimes deliberately disturb balance, break unity or flatten proportion for expressive effect, and folk and modernist works often ignore academic proportion altogether; the point is that the choice is deliberate and can be explained. To evaluate a work, ask what the artist has done with each principle, whether the eye travels where it is intended to travel, what the focal point is, and whether the whole feels resolved. That habit of analysis also improves your own studio decisions, because you can plan composition rather than discover its faults afterwards.
objectives: Define and identify the principles of design in given artworks
Explain how balance, emphasis, rhythm, contrast and unity work together in a composition
Plan and evaluate the composition of your own studio work using the principles

experiment.description: Composition Lab: Rearrange shapes in a frame to reach a chosen balance and emphasis, then compare with your own work.

lessons.title: Colour Theory and Application
lessons.content:
Colour has three measurable qualities. Hue is the name of the colour - red, yellow, blue, green. Value is how light or dark it is, made lighter by adding white (a tint) or darker by adding black or a complementary colour (a shade). Intensity, also called saturation or chroma, is how pure or greyed it is; mixing in a colour's opposite reduces its intensity and produces the dull, earthy tones and shadows that make other colours look brighter by comparison. In a subtractive medium such as paint, the primary colours that cannot be mixed are traditionally red, yellow and blue (in the printing process, cyan, magenta and yellow with black); mixing two primaries gives a secondary (orange, green, violet) and mixing a primary with an adjacent secondary gives a tertiary or intermediate colour. Colours lying opposite each other on the colour wheel are complementary (red and green, blue and orange, yellow and violet); those adjacent to each other are analogous. Complementary pairs placed together produce the strongest contrasts and, mixed together, neutralise each other - the practical answer to muddy colour. Warm colours (red, orange, yellow) appear to advance and create heat and energy; cool colours (blue, green, violet) recede and calm - a fact used in landscape painting to build depth.

Colour schemes are the deliberate groupings an artist uses. A monochromatic scheme uses one hue in varying values and intensities; analogous schemes use neighbouring hues and are naturally harmonious; complementary schemes use opposite hues for maximum contrast; split-complementary uses a hue with the two colours either side of its opposite; triadic schemes use three hues evenly spaced around the wheel; and earth palettes are built from ochres, umbers, siennas and greys, which suit Caribbean landscape, portrait and narrative work. Colour also carries meaning and mood, and that meaning is cultural and local: in Caribbean contexts green signals vegetation and vitality, gold and yellow the sun and carnival glitter, red both danger and celebration, white mourning in some traditions and purity in others, and African-derived colour symbolism still shapes mas and ritual work. Colour blindness, print production and lighting all change how a chosen palette is received, so colour choices are tested in the work itself.

Mixing and applying colour is a craft. Artists learn to mix on the palette in small quantities, to keep a clean water pot and cloth, to judge colour wet against dry because paint dries darker or duller, and to build a picture by laying in the broad masses first and refining later. Optical mixing - placing small strokes of different colours side by side so that the eye blends them - gives a livelier surface than mechanical mixing, and it is the technique behind impressionist and many Caribbean landscape surfaces. Glazing is done with transparent layers over dry paint, giving luminosity and depth; impasto uses thick paint, giving body and texture. Colour relationships must be judged against surrounding colour (never in isolation), and the same colour, next to another, will appear warmer, cooler, lighter or duller than it is. The most useful exercise is to paint the same subject with a limited palette, then with a contrasting one, and compare what the colour did to the meaning of the picture.
objectives: Describe hue, value and intensity and construct a colour wheel
Plan and apply monochromatic, analogous, complementary and triadic colour schemes
Mix and apply colour with glazing, optical mixing and impasto, considering local colour symbolism

experiment.description: Colour Mixer: Build a palette from a chosen scheme and mix each tint, shade and neutral step.

lessons.title: Painting Media and Techniques
lessons.content:
Each painting medium has its own character, and choosing the right one is part of designing the work. Watercolour is transparent, applied to paper with a brush and water; its lights are the paper itself, its darks come from layering, and it demands confidence because white cannot be added and hard edges cannot easily be removed - techniques include flat wash, graded wash, wet-on-wet (soft bleeding edges), wet-on-dry (crisp edges), dry brush, lifting out and masking. Gouache is opaque water-based paint used for poster-flat colour, illustration and design work. Acrylic dries quickly, is flexible, dries into a plastic film and can be used thinly like watercolour or thickly like oil; it adheres to almost any surface, so it serves mural and large-scale Caribbean work well, but its fast drying makes blending harder and requires cleaning before it sets. Oil paint is slow-drying, allowing blending, glazing and reworking over days, and has a rich depth of colour, but needs solvents, canvases and priming, and carries stronger health and safety demands. Tempera, posters, fabric paints (for batik and T-shirt printing), pastels and mixed media each bring their own effects and constraints.

Whatever the medium, the painting process follows a workable order. The surface is chosen and prepared for the job - stretched and primed canvas, paper taped to a board, board primed with gesso, or fabric washed and ironed; the composition is planned with a light drawing or a tonal underlayer (often raw umber or a warm grey); the broad masses of tone and colour are blocked in; then the work is developed in passes, from dark to light or light to dark depending on the medium, refining structure and edges and reserving the strongest contrast and sharpest detail for the focal point. Brushwork itself is expressive: a loaded flat brush gives a broad deliberate stroke, a round brush a drawn line, a dry brush a broken scratchy mark, a rigger a long thin line. Artists vary pressure, wetness, speed and tool to build surface interest, and they learn when to stop - overworked passages lose freshness and the evidence of the hand.

Finishing and care complete the work. Paint is allowed to dry properly (oils need months before varnishing), the work is signed, titled, dated and recorded, framed or mounted with an acid-free mount and hung out of direct sunlight; unframed works are protected between sheets of glassine or foam board. The studio must be managed for health and safety: good ventilation and extraction for solvents and sprays, masks when sanding or working with dust or pigments, gloves, no eating or drinking near materials, safe storage of flammables in a metal cabinet, careful disposal of rags and cleaning water, and correct labelling of containers - turpentine and white spirit are hazardous, and the pigments in some paints are toxic. A painting is also a document: keeping notes of media, support, palette and time taken is part of professional practice, and it is exactly what the SBA process journal requires.
objectives: Compare the properties, advantages and limitations of watercolour, gouache, acrylic and oil paint
Apply preparation, blocking-in, layering and finishing techniques appropriate to a chosen medium
Follow safe studio practice in the handling, storage and disposal of painting materials

experiment.description: Medium Matcher: Match a brief to the painting medium and technique that will achieve it best.

lessons.title: Drawing Media, Printmaking and Surface Design
lessons.content:
Drawing media are chosen for the marks they make. Graphite pencil is the most controllable, giving fine line and delicate tone from 9H (hard, light) to 9B (soft, dark); charcoal is soft, fast and dramatic, spreads and smudges easily and needs fixing; conte, pastel and chalk produce rich colour with a velvety surface; pen and ink gives permanent, decisive linear work, enlivened by hatching, cross-hatching and stippling for tone; felt-tipped and marker pens serve design drawing; and brush and ink combine drawn line with wash. Other media extend drawing - silverpoint, crayon, ballpoint, correction fluid for highlights, coffee and natural dyes, and collage of paper, fabric, foil and found objects. The choice affects the message: a charcoal figure study carries weight and immediacy, a fine pen drawing precision and delicacy, a pastel portrait warmth and softness. Drawing media also work together, and mixed-media work is standard in contemporary Caribbean practice.

Printmaking produces multiple original images from a prepared surface, and it demands thinking backwards, because the printed image is a mirror of the plate. Relief printing cuts away the areas that will stay white and prints the raised surface - lino and woodcut, cut with gouges and printed by hand or press; the technique suits bold, simplified shapes and is widely used in Caribbean schools and studios for high-contrast social and folk imagery. Intaglio printing cuts or etches lines into a plate, fills them with ink and wipes the surface clean, printing from the incised lines under great pressure - drypoint, etching, aquatint. Planographic printing prints from a flat stone or plate, in which grease and water repel each other - the lithograph. Stencil and screen printing (serigraphy) force ink through a masked screen and are the basis of T-shirt, poster, packaging and Carnival printing, allowing multiple colours by registering several screens. Monotype and monoprint produce single unique impressions from a painted or inked surface. Editions are numbered (for example 3/25, the third of twenty-five), signed and dated, and the plate is destroyed or marked after the edition is complete, because the artist's promise of limited numbers is part of the artwork's value.

Surface design applies similar thinking to cloth and other materials, and it is central to Caribbean visual culture. Batik uses wax resist applied to fabric which is then dyed; the waxed areas resist the dye, and repeated waxing and dyeing build layers of colour, with the wax cracked deliberately for the characteristic veined line. Tie-dye binds or folds cloth to resist dye in patterns, and other resists include starch, glue and stencils. Direct techniques - hand-painting fabric, block printing with carved stamps, screen printing, applique, embroidery, patchwork and quilting - produce everything from household textiles to fashion. Printmaking and surface design both require an orderly workshop: sharp tools stored safely, cutting away from the body, proper ventilation for solvents, protective gloves and aprons for dyes, careful handling of hot wax and irons, and clean-up of inks and chemicals - because the processes that make beautiful surfaces also carry real hazards.
objectives: Select and combine drawing media for a stated intention
Explain relief, intaglio, planographic and stencil printing and produce a simple print
Apply resist and direct surface-design techniques to fabric safely

experiment.description: Print Studio: Design a two-colour relief print, reverse the plate in your mind and plan the cutting steps.

lessons.title: Sculpture and Three-Dimensional Construction
lessons.content:
Sculpture is art in three dimensions, and it is made by four broad processes. Carving is subtractive: material is removed from wood, stone, plaster or a block of composition material with gouges, chisels, mallets and files, and the artist works with the grain and structure of the material, since a mistake cannot be replaced. Modelling is additive: soft material such as clay, plasticine, wax or papier-mache is built up, pushed and smoothed, and it is the most forgiving method because material can be added or removed at will. Casting reproduces a modelled form in another material, usually by making a mould (often in plaster or silicone) and pouring in plaster, resin, cement or molten metal; waste-mould and piece-mould methods allow complex forms, and lost-wax casting is the traditional route to bronze. Construction and assemblage assemble the work from separate pieces - welded, soldered, glued, bolted, nailed or tied - using wood, metal, plastics, glass, paper, rope, textile and found or recycled objects; because the material need not be traditional, this is the most open method and the basis of much modern and environmental Caribbean work using plastic bottles, tyres, driftwood and scrap metal.

Three-dimensional design must be considered in the round, because a sculpture has no single front. Volume and mass describe how much space the form displaces and how heavy it feels; open form (space flowing through, as in a wire or welded piece) reads as light, and closed form as solid. Along with mass, the sculptor uses line, plane, texture, colour and scale, and must solve structural problems: weight, balance (a standing figure needs the centre of gravity over its base), joining, armature or internal support, and the mounts or plinth that carry the finished work. Scale changes meaning - a hand-sized figure invites handling, a life-sized one confronts the viewer, a monumental public work occupies a whole site. Light matters as much in sculpture as in painting: a form is read through the shadows it casts and receives, which is why maquettes and finished works are judged in changing daylight, and why public sculptures are usually designed for their surroundings, whether a busy roundabout, a school compound or a gallery floor.

Studio safety and finishing complete the work. Carving tools are sharp and are always cut away from the body, with the workpiece clamped; stone carving produces harmful dust, so masks, ventilation and wet working are required; wood dust, resin fumes, glue vapour, welding sparks and metal filings each demand their own protection; and materials must be stored and disposed of properly. Finishing involves cleaning the surface, sanding, filling, sealing, painting, waxing, patination or applying a protective coating, and mounting the work on an appropriate base with the title, date, medium and signature recorded. Documentation is part of the artist's practice: photographing the work from several angles, noting dimensions, materials and process, and writing about the decisions made. For the SBA and for a career, that record is what allows a piece to be exhibited, explained, insured, priced and sold.
objectives: Describe carving, modelling, casting, construction and assemblage and choose a method for a brief
Analyse form in three dimensions: mass, volume, balance, structure, texture, scale and viewpoint
Finish, mount and document a sculpture safely

experiment.description: Sculpt Bench: Choose a method and material for a brief, then test where the centre of gravity must sit.

lessons.title: Ceramics and Clay Work
lessons.content:
Clay is the most widely available sculptural material and the basis of pottery, and working with it requires understanding its properties. Clay is plastic when moist, can be shaped, joined and textured, becomes leather-hard as it dries, is fragile and can be broken while bone dry, and is permanently changed by firing in a kiln. Types include earthenware (low-firing, porous, soft, the traditional terracotta of Caribbean potters), stoneware (higher-firing, dense and durable), porcelain (fine, white, translucent, high-firing and difficult) and raku and other special clays; clay bodies may be smooth or grogged with fired clay particles to add texture and reduce shrinkage problems. Preparing clay means wedging or kneading it to remove air pockets and even out moisture; air trapped inside a thick wall will expand in the kiln and destroy the piece, which is why walls are made even and hollow forms are opened before firing. Shrinkage - often around ten per cent from wet to fired - must be allowed for in the design.

Hand-building is the entry into ceramics. Pinching forms a pot from a ball of clay pressed with the thumb; coiling builds walls from rolled ropes of clay joined with score-and-slip (roughening both surfaces and using slip, a liquid clay, as glue); slab building joins flat rolled sheets into boxes, tiles and angular forms; press moulding pushes clay into or over a mould; and extruding forces clay through a shaped die. Throwing on a potter's wheel is the skilled method of raising cylindrical and rounded forms from a centred lump of clay, and turning and trimming refine the base afterwards. Decoration may be applied at different stages: impressing, stamping, incising and sgraffito while the clay is soft; attaching handles, spouts and modelled elements with score-and-slip; and adding texture with tools, textiles or found objects. Handles and appendages must be joined well or they fall off in the kiln or in use, and every join is a potential crack.

Finishing and firing make clay permanent. Once leather-hard the work is trimmed and smoothed; when bone dry it is loaded into the kiln for a bisque firing, which is slow to avoid steam explosions. Surfaces may then be left bare, painted with slip or underglaze, glazed (dipped, poured or brushed) or coated with oxides, and a second, higher glaze firing fuses the glaze into a glass-like surface. Glazes can be glossy, matt, crystalline, crackled or textured, and they interact with the clay body and the firing temperature, so potters keep records of every recipe and firing, as a glaze is chemistry rather than guesswork. Beyond the studio, ceramics offers Caribbean artists work in tableware, tiles, sculpture, water filters, planters and souvenir production - a genuine small-business route - and it carries real hazards: silica dust from dry clay and glaze materials must not be inhaled (no dry sweeping, use wet cleaning and masks), kilns are extremely hot and need clear space and correct ventilation, glazes containing lead or other toxic metals must be handled with care, and kilns must be sited where children and the public cannot touch them.
objectives: Explain clay types, preparation, shrinkage and the stages of working clay
Use hand-building methods and wheel throwing to make a form, and join and decorate it soundly
Describe bisque and glaze firing, glaze application and safe ceramic studio practice

experiment.description: Kiln Scheduler: Plan the stages from wet clay to glazed pot and find the step where the piece would fail.

lessons.title: Caribbean Craft Traditions and Applied Art
lessons.content:
Caribbean art is not confined to galleries: it lives in baskets, mats, hammocks, hats, calabash engravings, drums, jewellery, furniture, ironwork, batik, Carnival costumes and everyday objects, and much of it carries knowledge brought from Africa, Asia, Europe and the region's indigenous peoples. Fibre and straw craft - weaving and plaiting palm, sisal, cane, cotton, jippi-jappa, banana and palm trash into baskets, mats, fans, hats and bags - is practised across the region, and the techniques are mathematical as well as visual: the pattern depends on count, warp and weft, and the shape is formed by increasing and decreasing. Leather work, wood carving and furniture making, calabash and gourd decoration, beadwork, wire bending, tinsmithing, maracas and drums, and metal sculpture from discarded machinery all continue as living traditions, and apprenticeship and family transmission remain central to how the skills move between generations.

Textile and mas arts are the region's most visible applied art. Carnival and Junkanoo costume work combines structural engineering with decoration: a frame of wire, cane, bamboo or aluminium carries feathers, fabric, beads, sequins, glitter and paint, and the builder must balance structure, weight, comfort, mobility and spectacle for a performer who may dance for hours. Design skills required include sketching the costume, working at scale, choosing colour for impact on a parade route at night, costing materials for a band of hundreds, and managing a construction team. Batik, tie-dye, applique, patchwork and screen-printed textiles supply clothing, home furnishings and souvenir markets; screen printing and digital printing serve the same purpose industrially. Carnival-arts practitioners are professionals in their own right, and many combine costume building with fashion, set design, teaching and tourism performance work.

Contemporary applied artists build enterprises on these traditions, and the practical concerns of a craft business are as important as the making: costing materials and time, pricing for profit rather than for approval, choosing markets and channels (craft markets, shops, hotels, festivals, online stores, export through regional craft bodies), keeping products consistent while remaining handmade, presenting work with stories that explain its origin and meaning, protecting designs where the law allows, and using appropriate materials that will last and ship safely. Sustainability is now part of the value: work made from recycled wire, glass, plastic and fabric appeals to buyers and reduces waste. The craft sector, small as its individual businesses are, is a real employer across the Caribbean, and it is the reason that courses in Visual Arts treat craft, design and fine art as one field rather than opposites.
objectives: Describe Caribbean craft traditions in fibre, leather, wood, metal and textile
Explain the design and construction demands of Carnival costume building
Cost, price, market and present craft products as a small business

experiment.description: Craft Costing: Cost a handmade item, set a price and see whether the item makes a profit at market day.

title: Graphic Design, Illustration and Digital Media

lessons.title: Graphic Design: Layout, Typography and Identity
lessons.content:
Graphic design is visual communication: it solves a problem - announce, inform, persuade, identify, warn or entertain - by arranging type, image, colour and space. The process begins with the brief, which states the client, the purpose, the audience, the message, the format, the deadline and the budget. Research follows: what the audience already knows and how they read, what competitors produce, what imagery and language will be understood. Then come thumbnail sketches by the dozen, from which a few roughs are developed at actual size, refined into comprehensives, tested on real people, and approved before production. Design decisions are always judged against the purpose, not against personal preference, which is why designers present options with reasons rather than a single fait accompli.

Layout organises the surface. A grid divides the format into columns, margins and fields so that elements line up and the design holds together whether it is a poster, a leaflet, a web page or a book page; asymmetric and modular grids allow variety while keeping order. Hierarchy tells the eye what to read first, second and third, using size, weight, position, colour and white space - the headline shouts, the subheading explains, the body informs, the small print complies. White space is an active element, giving the eye rest and making the emphasis work; cramped pages lose both clarity and elegance. Typography supplies the voice: serif faces read as traditional and formal, sans-serif as modern and neutral, script faces as personal, and display faces as loud; type must be legible at its final size, limited to two or three families, and set with attention to point size, leading (line spacing), letter and word spacing, alignment, measure (line length), and hierarchy of styles. Widows, orphans, bad rag, rivers and poor hyphenation are corrected in the final pass, because type errors destroy credibility faster than readers can say why.

Identity design builds a lasting visual signature. A logo must be simple, memorable, appropriate, versatile (working in one colour, at postage-stamp size and on a billboard), distinctive and durable, and it is developed alongside a colour palette, typeface selection, imagery style and rules for use - an identity system that keeps a school, business, festival or band recognisable on everything from letterheads and signs to jerseys and social media. Layout work is produced manually or digitally, and print production demands technical knowledge: resolution (300 dpi for print), colour mode (CMYK for print, RGB for screen), bleed and crop marks, paper stock, finishing, and file formats for the printer. Designers must also respect copyright in images and typefaces, use licensed fonts, credit photographers and illustrators, and obtain model and property releases where needed - because a beautiful design built on stolen or unlicensed material is a liability, not an asset.
objectives: Work through a design brief from research and thumbnails to a finished layout
Apply grid, hierarchy, white space and typography principles to a chosen format
Design a simple visual identity and prepare artwork correctly for print or screen

experiment.description: Layout Grid: Place headline, image and body copy on a grid to a brief and check hierarchy and legibility.

lessons.title: Illustration, Storytelling and Visual Narrative
lessons.content:
Illustration is image made to explain, illuminate or narrate. It works with text rather than replacing it: an illustration can show what the text cannot say quickly, describe what is too large, small, dangerous or distant to photograph, express mood, and give a story a face. Illustration serves books, textbooks, newspapers, magazines, advertising, packaging, posters, comics, graphic novels, animation, games, greeting cards and public information campaigns, and in the Caribbean it is central to children's publishing, cultural education and campaigning work on health and environment. The illustrator's first task is reading: identifying the passage or message to be illustrated, the audience's age and understanding, the page size and position, the printing or screen constraints, and the mood the piece must carry.

Visual storytelling has its own grammar. Character design fixes appearance, age, costume, proportion and expression so that a character is recognisable across many drawings; expression and body language carry emotion more powerfully than words; composition and framing decide what the reader notices, using close-up for tension, wide shot for setting, high and low angles for vulnerability or power; light and colour set atmosphere and time of day; and sequence, pacing and page layout control how the eye moves through a story, which is the particular craft of the comic and graphic novel. Panels, gutters, speech balloons, thought bubbles, captions and sound effects form a symbolic vocabulary, and a storyboard plans the sequence of images before the finished artwork is produced - the same discipline used in film, animation and advertising. Thumbnails, roughs and character sheets are working documents, not waste paper, and editors expect to see them.

Illustrators work in traditional and digital media, often together: pencil, ink and wash, watercolour, gouache, acrylic, collage, linocut for a bold graphic character, and pen and ink for detailed line work; then scanning, digital colouring, tablet drawing and vector or raster software for production. Style is developed by studying admired illustrators and Caribbean visual traditions, and by drawing constantly from life - because invented figures that were never observed look weak, while a sketchbook habit makes every commission easier. Commercially, illustration is a business: work is quoted on the scope of the brief, licensing terms state how the image may be used, territory, duration and exclusivity, the artist retains copyright unless it is explicitly assigned in writing, and files are supplied to a printer's specification with correct resolution and colour mode. Reputation is built on meeting deadlines, taking notes well, revising without complaint and delivering clean files - the same professionalism expected of any worker.
objectives: Plan and produce illustrations that illuminate a given text for a stated audience
Use character design, framing, light and sequence to tell a story visually
Explain copyright, licensing and professional practice in illustration work

experiment.description: Storyboard Lab: Turn a short folk tale into six panels and pick the framing for each.

lessons.title: Photography and Digital Art
lessons.content:
Photography is a visual art that begins with the camera and ends with an image, and the first decisions are compositional. A photograph has a subject, and the photographer chooses what to include and what to leave out by framing - moving closer, changing height, choosing vertical or horizontal format and simplifying the background. Composition applies the same principles as drawing: the rule of thirds places points of interest away from the centre where the eye rests, leading lines carry the viewer inwards, framing devices such as doorways and branches enclose the subject, repetition and pattern create rhythm, and perspective, depth and scale give the image structure. Balance of light and shadow, colour temperature (the warm orange of evening and cool blue of shade), and the quality of light - hard sunlight against soft overcast or shaded light - change the mood of the same subject entirely. Caribbean photographers work with intense midday sun, where early morning and late afternoon light is far more flattering than the flat glare of noon.

Technique controls the image. Exposure is the balance of three settings: aperture, which controls the size of the lens opening, governs depth of field (a small aperture keeps foreground and background both sharp; a wide aperture throws the background out of focus); shutter speed decides whether movement is frozen or blurred; and ISO measures sensitivity to light, raising noise as it rises. Focal length (wide-angle, standard, telephoto) changes the relationship between subject and background, and macro and close-up work reveals detail invisible to the eye. Beyond the technical, the camera is used deliberately: documentary photography records people, work and social conditions; portrait photography depends on trust and expression; landscape and architecture celebrate place; street and event photography capture the unrepeatable moment; and photography also serves as source material, as every painter's reference file shows. Photographers must also consider consent, privacy, cultural sensitivity and the way they represent the communities they photograph.

Digital work extends from editing to creation. Images are imported, catalogued and backed up; then edited for cropping, straightening, exposure, contrast, colour balance, retouching, selective sharpening and conversion to black and white, in a workflow that saves a working copy and never destroys the original. Composite and digital painting work requires layers, masks, blend modes, brushes and tablet control, and the principles of painting and composition apply exactly as they do to a canvas - layer palettes and brush settings are only new tools, not new rules. Output matters as much as capture: images are prepared for screen (RGB, lower resolution, sRGB profile, sensible file size) or for print (CMYK or high-resolution RGB, 300 dpi at final size, correct paper profile), and they are presented in exhibitions as framed prints, in portfolios as ordered sequences, and online as galleries and social media feeds with captions and credits. Digital artists must also respect the law and each other: copyright applies to photographs and digital images exactly as to paintings, stock images are used under licence, subjects give consent, and editing does not extend to deceiving viewers about events or people.
objectives: Compose photographs using framing, the rule of thirds, lines and light
Explain aperture, shutter speed, ISO and depth of field and their creative effects
Edit, output and present digital images and observe copyright, consent and ethical practice

experiment.description: Camera Lab: Set aperture, shutter speed and ISO for a brief and predict the look of the result.

lessons.title: Indigenous, Ancestral and Folk Art Traditions
lessons.content:
The visual culture of the Caribbean begins long before European arrival. The Taino and other indigenous peoples of the Greater and Lesser Antilles carved and incised duhos (ceremonial seats), cemis and zemis (spirit figures and images) in wood, stone, bone and shell, made pottery with modelled faces and painted decoration, worked gold and guanin alloys, and created body art, cotton textiles and baskets with geometric patterns. Petroglyphs and pictographs carved into rock faces survive across the region, and archaeological ceramics give evidence of how motifs travelled between islands. Caribbean art history therefore starts with indigenous visual language, and contemporary artists draw on these forms deliberately - not as decoration but as a way of reconnecting with a pre-colonial inheritance that colonisation suppressed.

African heritage is the largest single source of the region's visual vocabulary. Enslaved and later indentured Africans carried knowledge of carving, weaving, ironwork, pottery, drum-making and textiles, and those skills survived and adapted: the Adinkra-like symbolism and geometric patterning of some Caribbean craft, the importance of the drum as both instrument and sculpture, ironwork traditions in Haiti and Jamaica, the strip-weaving and applique techniques of textile work, and the ritual objects, flags and costumes of Afro-Caribbean religious and festival practice. East Indian indentured workers brought the patterns, colours and techniques of Indian textiles, jewellery, embroidery and architecture; Chinese and Middle Eastern communities added further traditions; and European colonial styles were absorbed and altered in local building, furniture and church decoration. The result is not a mixture but a set of living traditions, each with its own community, purpose and rules of practice.

Folk and popular art traditions are where Caribbean visual culture is most visible. Junkanoo and Carnival, with their wire-bent frames, crepe paper, fabric, bead and feather work, are a form of temporary monumental sculpture and textile art rebuilt every year, and they absorb extraordinary skill in design, construction and performance. Yard and garden art, painted shop signs and murals, hand-painted barbers' and rum-shop signs, house and gate decoration, gravestone carving, religious banners, obeah and ritual objects, handmade toys, calabash engraving and utility craft all carry aesthetic intention outside the gallery system. Many of the artists now celebrated began in these traditions, and the study of folk art asks not whether it follows academic rules but what it means to the community that makes and uses it. Appreciation also brings responsibility: borrowing motifs from a tradition that is not your own requires understanding, credit and, where possible, collaboration.
objectives: Describe the art forms of the indigenous peoples of the Caribbean
Trace African, Asian and European influences in Caribbean craft and design
Explain the aesthetic and cultural role of folk, religious and festival art

experiment.description: Motif Tracer: Follow a motif from one tradition to another and note how its meaning changes.

lessons.title: National Art Movements and Major Artists
lessons.content:
From the 1920s the Caribbean developed movements that deliberately set out to picture the region and its people in their own terms. In Jamaica the emerging nationalist current of the 1930s and 1940s produced an art movement around the sculptor Edna Manley, whose work and teaching insisted that the Jamaican labourer and peasant had monumental dignity; she was instrumental in founding the art school that became the Edna Manley College of the Visual and Performing Arts, and her circle included Albert Huie, whose market and landscape paintings made ordinary Jamaican life the subject of serious art, and Barrington Watson, Ralph Campbell, Osmond Watson and Karl Parboosingh, who studied abroad and brought back figure painting, expressionism and abstraction in Caribbean subjects. Alongside the academic line grew the so-called Intuitives - self-taught artists including Mallica 'Kapo' Reynolds, whose visionary paintings and carvings mix religion, healing and colour, and Everald Brown, whose densely patterned work binds Rastafarian and biblical imagery to Jamaican landscape. David Pottinger, Sidney McLaren, Albert Artwell and others extended the movement, and the National Gallery of Jamaica began collecting and exhibiting this work as a national inheritance.

Other Caribbean territories produced their own movements in the same decades. In Trinidad, Boscoe Holder, Geoffrey Holder, Sybil Atteck, Carlisle Chang, M. P. Alladin and Leroy Clarke built a tradition of figurative, folk and abstract work rooted in carnival, Hindu and African Caribbean life; the Trinidad art society and later the national museum and gallery created institutions to sustain it. Haiti's heights of popular painting - "naive" or "primitive" work from the Centre d'Art tradition, including artists such as Hector Hyppolite, Philome Obin and Préfète Duffaut - became internationally known and remain a major contribution to world art. Cuba's modern movement, with Wifredo Lam linking African ritual imagery with European modernism, and Barbados, Guyana (Aubrey Williams, Denis Williams), St Lucia (Derek Walcott's visual work as well as his theatre), Suriname and the francophone Caribbean each added distinctive currents. Common threads run through them: landscape used as identity rather than scenery, the human figure as subject, colour used boldly, folk and religious imagery reclaimed as fine art, and politics - colonialism, labour, migration, independence - present whether implicit or explicit.

Since independence, Caribbean art has diversified into abstraction, installation, video, performance, digital work and diaspora practice, while the market and institutional base has grown: national galleries, the biennials of Havana, Santo Domingo and elsewhere, the Jamaica Biennial, commercial galleries, art fairs, auctions and increasingly online sales, plus a diaspora market that buys both traditional subjects and contemporary work. Studying these artists is not memorising names but understanding choices: whose faces and places are depicted, what materials and forms are used, how gender, class, race, migration and nationhood are handled, and how a local movement engages international art without losing its own voice. For your own practice, the useful question is which of these approaches gives you a language for what you see around you.
objectives: Identify major Caribbean artists, their works and their contribution
Explain how Caribbean art movements responded to colonialism, identity and independence
Analyse a chosen artwork's subject, form, materials and meaning in context

experiment.description: Art Timeline: Place Caribbean artworks and movements on a timeline and link each to a social change.

lessons.title: Art in Society, Exhibiting and the Law
lessons.content:
Art does social work. In the Caribbean it marks religious observance and national celebration, teaches and warns on public health issues, commemorates national heroes and historical events, decorates public buildings, schools and transport, and contributes to tourism, festivals, film, advertising and publishing. Institutions support it: the ministry responsible for culture, national galleries and museums, arts councils, the schools and colleges that teach it, festivals such as CARIFESTA, community arts bodies, and the regional and international organisations that fund exchange and training. Private patronage comes from collectors, businesses that buy or commission work, hotels and attractions, banks, and increasingly from online buyers. Understanding who funds and shows art - and on what terms - helps an artist make a living without being exploited.

Exhibiting is the public act of showing work, and it is planned like any other production. The artist or curator decides on a theme and a selection of works, writes a statement and captions, and considers the sequence and the space; the gallery or venue handles lighting, hanging, labels and security; and the opening, catalogue, press release, invitations, price list and guest book are prepared in advance. Hanging requires attention to sight lines, height (typically at eye level), spacing, lighting and protective measures; works are labelled with title, artist, year, medium, dimensions and price; and assistants explain and handle sales, take deposits, issue receipts and record buyers. Practical arrangements matter to reputation: works arrive on time, framed and ready to hang, with a signed consignment list stating prices and commission, a clear agreement about insurance and who bears the risk, and transport and packing arrangements suited to the work. An exhibition is also a set of relationships, and courtesy, punctuality and follow-up after the show - receipts, thanks, payments, collection of unsold work - build the reputation that leads to the next show.

Law and ethics protect the artist's work and the public's rights. Copyright arises automatically when an original work is created and fixed (painted, drawn, photographed, recorded, stored digitally); it protects the form of expression, not the idea, and it lasts for the life of the creator plus a period of years that varies by territory. Rights include reproduction, distribution, public performance and display, adaptation and the moral rights of attribution and integrity - the right to be named and to object to treatment of your work that would harm your reputation. A commission or sale should be in writing, stating the price, scope, deadline, approval stages, who owns the physical work, whether copyright is licensed or assigned, and whether the artist may reproduce the image; that last point matters greatly, because a muralist or illustrator who signs away all rights loses the ability to use the work in a portfolio or to license it. Contracts, invoices, delivery notes and insurance are not bureaucracy - they are how artists get paid, recover unpaid fees and keep their work intact. There are limits and responsibilities in the other direction too: artists must not copy or closely imitate another's work, must have permission and consent for images of people, and must respect cultural sensitivity in what they depict.
objectives: Explain the roles of galleries, festivals, patrons and government in the arts
Plan, hang, label and document an exhibition with correct professional arrangements
Explain copyright, moral rights, contracts and ethical duties relating to artworks

experiment.description: Gallery Planner: Select works, plan the hang and write the labels and price list for a small show.

lessons.title: The Sketchbook, Process Journal and Research
lessons.content:
A sketchbook is the artist's studio in miniature: a place to look, think, try, fail and record. It should be used every day, not only when work is going well, because its value is cumulative. Useful content includes observational drawing from life - objects, people, buildings, plants, hands, animals; quick gesture studies and longer tonal drawings; experiments with media, papers, tools and techniques, with notes on what happened; colour studies, palettes and mixing tests; thumbnail compositions and alternative arrangements of the same subject; copied and adapted passages from artists you admire, clearly credited; photographs, ticket stubs, fabric, leaves and other collected material collaged in; written notes, questions, quotations and lists; and dated entries showing the development of an idea over weeks. A sketchbook is not a finished object and should not be neatened into uselessness: crossing out, scribbling, working over a drawing and annotating are evidence of thinking, which is exactly what assessors and gallery directors look for.

The process journal is the written companion to the sketchbook and, in CSEC Visual Arts, it is assessed work. For each piece it records the stimulus or theme, the research carried out, the visual references and artists studied, the development of ideas through sketches and trials, the media, techniques and processes used, the problems encountered and the solutions found, the time taken, the final outcome, and an honest evaluation of what succeeded and what would be done differently. Research is a practical activity: visit galleries, studios, markets, churches, festivals and public buildings; interview craftspeople, artisans and artists; photograph and sketch on site; read books and reliable online sources and record the details; and keep everything dated and sourced, because an unsourced idea is unverifiable and an uncited image is a risk to your marks and to your integrity. A journal with specific, dated, illustrated entries demonstrates a working process; a journal filled in the week before submission never convinces anyone.

Documentation protects the work you produce. Photograph each finished piece in good even light against a plain background, with and without a scale or measure, and store full-resolution files, plus the sketches, so that a digital portfolio exists even if the physical work is damaged, sold or lost; record title, date, medium, dimensions, price and any sale; keep the working files, source images and licences for digital work; and back everything up in more than one place, including cloud storage. Write a short artist's statement - a few hundred words on what you make, why, how, and what tradition you work in - because it is required for exhibitions, applications, study and social media, and because writing it forces clarity about your own practice. Finally, organise the studio so the habit can survive: a permanent workspace, tools and materials within reach, work in progress protected, materials labelled, and a stock of prepared boards, paper and canvas so that a free hour can be spent making work rather than setting up.
objectives: Keep a comprehensive, dated sketchbook and process journal
Carry out and cite visual research and record the development of an idea
Photograph, catalogue and back up finished work and write an artist's statement

experiment.description: Journal Check: Review a set of journal entries and identify which stages of the process are missing.

lessons.title: Planning and Producing the SBA Portfolio
lessons.content:
The Visual Arts SBA is a body of practical work with a supporting journal, and it is planned backwards from the deadline. The first step is to understand the requirements exactly - how many pieces, which areas or components must be covered, the size and media expectations, the deadlines for submission stages and the marking criteria - and then to build a work plan that fits the terms, holidays and examination periods remaining. Each piece is planned as a project: the theme and intention, the research and references, the compositional thumbnails, the choice of media and support, the stages of execution with realistic time allowances, and the display or mounting requirements. A plan of twelve pieces each needing three hours of unfinished work at the end of term is a plan to fail; a plan with weekly targets, buffer time and the riskiest pieces scheduled first is a plan that survives illness, power cuts, rain and other subjects.

Producing work to a standard involves craft discipline. Supports are prepared properly - paper stretched or taped flat, canvas primed, board sealed, clay wedged, frames of wire or cane built for mas or sculptural work; media are tested on the same surface before commitment; drawings are transferred and composition is checked at arm's length and in a mirror; progress is photographed; and unfinished work is protected from dust, sun, damp, insects and careless handling. Finished work is allowed to dry properly, signed and dated where appropriate, titled, and mounted or framed with care - using acid-free mount board, a window mount or a proper frame, labels that state title, medium, size, date and the artist's name, and protective packing for transport. Consistency of presentation matters because an exhibition or portfolio is judged as a whole: mismatched mounts and hurried labelling undermine good work. Assessors and curators look for evidence of an idea pursued rather than a scatter of unrelated exercises, so a portfolio should show development - a body of work with a theme, a range of media and approaches, and a clear progression from simpler to more ambitious pieces.

Presentation is the final stage of the work, not an afterthought. For an exhibition, works are selected and sequenced, the space measured and the hang planned with sight lines and lighting in mind, labels and an artist's statement are prepared, prices and a guest list are decided, and the opening is organised. For a portfolio submission, work may be presented physically in a sturdy portfolio case with tissue interleaving, or digitally as a designed PDF and online gallery with high-resolution images, captions and a contents page; both must be complete, clean and labelled so that the assessor can find everything without asking. The journal accompanies the practical work and is the evidence that the work was yours and was made through research and reflection. Finally, look after the physical record: photograph everything before submission, keep the digital copies safe, and collect the work promptly afterwards, since the portfolio becomes the core of your application for further study, exhibitions and paid commissions.
objectives: Plan a portfolio programme against the SBA requirements and deadlines
Produce, prepare, mount and label work to a consistent professional standard
Present a portfolio physically and digitally with all supporting documentation

experiment.description: Portfolio Planner: Lay out a term's work plan, spot the overloaded weeks and rebalance before you begin.

lessons.title: Careers, Enterprise and Safe Studio Practice
lessons.content:
Visual arts training leads to many kinds of work, and students should know the range. Fine artists produce and exhibit work for sale through galleries, art fairs, online stores and commissions, often combining this with teaching, workshops and residencies. Designers work in graphic, web, product, interior, fashion, textile, costume, exhibition and set design for businesses, agencies, printers, broadcasters and cultural institutions. Illustrators and photographers serve publishing, advertising, editorial, animation, games and documentation; animators and digital artists work in film, television, advertising and games studios. Craftspeople and applied artists make ceramics, textiles, jewellery, furniture, batik and Carnival costume; muralists, sign-painters, tattoo artists and restorers practise specific trades; art teachers and lecturers work in schools and colleges; and arts administration offers roles in galleries, museums, festivals, arts councils and cultural agencies. Around all of these sit the supporting trades: framing, printing, art supply, art transport and installation, and conservation. Many artists combine several of these - a common Caribbean pattern is teaching or public service, plus commissioned work, plus studio practice, plus design jobs.

Making a living requires business skills as well as craft. Cost the work honestly: materials, an hourly rate for your time, studio overheads, framing, transport, insurance, a share for the gallery or agent and tax, then set a price that allows a discount without a loss and that you can hold consistently across buyers and markets. Keep records - invoices, receipts, expenses, sales, contracts - and register and pay tax as required, because professional paperwork is what separates a business from a hobby and what protects you in a dispute. Marketing is showing the work and telling its story: a portfolio and artist's statement, a website and social media feed with good photography and regular posting, participation in exhibitions, markets and festivals, relationships with galleries, designers, hotels, tourism bodies and businesses that commission, and a mailing list of buyers and supporters. Contracts should be in writing, stating scope, price, deadline, revisions, ownership of the physical work, copyright and licensing terms, and what happens if the client cancels; a deposit of a third to a half is normal for commissions; and unpaid fees can be pursued through a small claims court or by withholding delivery, since copyright remains yours unless assigned. Many artists find the safest path is to diversify income streams - commissions, teaching, design work, product sales, workshops and grants - rather than rely on one.

Health and safety is a professional obligation in every studio, because art materials can injure. Solvents such as turpentine, white spirit, thinners and aerosol sprays give off harmful vapour: they are used with the window open, extraction on, in small quantities, with the lid replaced, and never with a source of ignition nearby; paints, glazes, dyes, resins and adhesives may contain lead, cadmium, cobalt, formaldehyde or other toxins, so gloves are worn, skin contact avoided, and containers labelled and stored according to their safety data; dust from clay, plaster, stone, wood and sanding is a serious hazard and is controlled by wet working, extraction, sealed containers and masks, and dry sweeping is avoided; kilns, welding equipment, soldering irons, hot wax and laminators burn, so they are sited safely, never left unattended, and used with correct handling and fire equipment nearby. Sharp tools - knives, gouges, chisels, guillotines, needle tools - are kept sharp (blunt tools cause more injuries), cut away from the body, used on a proper surface with the workpiece clamped, and stored safely. Work posture and load are planned: easels and tables at correct height, heavy boards and sculptures lifted with the legs, moved on trolleys or with help. And the studio has rules for everyone in it - no eating or drinking where materials are handled, hands washed before touching food, aprons and closed shoes worn, waste paints and solvents disposed of according to local regulations rather than poured down a drain, and a first-aid kit, fire extinguisher and clear exit kept where they can be reached. Safe practice is not fussiness: a career in art requires functioning hands, lungs and eyes for several decades.
objectives: Describe the range of careers and income streams available to visual artists
Cost and price work, keep business records and use written agreements and marketing
Identify studio hazards and apply safe practice for materials, tools, dust, heat and waste

experiment.description: Studio Safety: Inspect a listed studio set-up, identify each hazard and choose the control that fixes it.
